t: How A One-Second Strategy Can Motivate Your New Class
q: For years I’ve had a poster on my classroom door that reads “Learn Like A Champion Today.” Each student taps it on their way in.
But the act of tapping it, the decision to reach up and give it a rap, is where you’ll find its power. It’s the meaning behind the action that makes it work.
You must walk your students outside your classroom during the first week of school and, while modeling how you want them to enter, explain that by tapping the poster they're agreeing to three things.
Because it must be entirely their choice. If it isn’t, if you force your students to tap it or glare at them when they don’t, then it loses its power. It no longer possesses any meaning.

t: 9 Ways To Have More Authority Next School Year https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/07/22/9-ways-to-have-more-authority-next-school-year/
q: Although, at first glance, authority appears to be an inborn gift reserved for a lucky few, there is really no mystery at all.
This one is huge. Do what you say you’re going to do and over time your authority will skyrocket.
The appearance of confidence can have the same effect. According to research, simply changing your posture can make you feel more powerful and thus behave more confidently.
Lecturing, glaring, scolding, and losing your cool may frighten students into behaving in the short term, but the price is your respect, plummeting authority, and more and more misbehavior.
Nervous energy has a way of spreading throughout the classroom, infecting every inch. It causes excitability, inattentiveness, and a form of misbehavior that is very difficult to eliminate.
But the truth is, it’s nothing more than a set of traits available to anyone. They’re available to anyone willing to adopt them for themself and dare to be more than just another teacher.

t: 3 Promises For The First Day Of School
q: Of the many items on your first-day-of-school checklist, three promises should go at the very top.
The promises should be delivered with boldness and sincerity and within the first 20 minutes of meeting your new class.
Depending on your grade level, it may include how you’ll never raise your voice in anger or how you’ll never threaten, scold, or manipulate or how you’ll never use sarcasm or cut down to size.
This is the ultimate promise that protects their right to learn and enjoy school. Thus, you must frame everything you say about why you’re so faithful to it in these terms.
You also put yourself on record—and your reputation on the line—which exerts just enough pressure to ensure your consistent follow through.
The promises are a statement of belief—in yourself, in them, and in the transformational power of great teaching.
x: Michael Linsin recommends three explicit promises teachers should make to their class within the first twenty minutes of the school year: a promise to treat students with respect, defined concretely as never raising…
Three specific promises — respect, listening/protection, and faithful adherence to the classroom management plan — should be delivered boldly within the first twenty minutes of the school year.
The respect promise should be defined in concrete behavioral terms: never raising one's voice, threatening, scolding, or using sarcasm.
The management-plan promise should be framed entirely around how it protects students' right to learn and enjoy school, not as a rules announcement.
Publicly committing to these promises creates self-imposed accountability pressure that helps ensure the teacher's own follow-through.
Linsin also notes that publicly committing to these promises creates accountability pressure on the teacher, reinforcing their own consistency.

t: How To Be Both Calm And Enthusiastic Next School Year
q: A calm disposition can sweep excitability right out of your classroom. It can improve listening and attentiveness. It can curb misbehavior and accelerate maturity.
Calmness, of the kind that permeates the classroom and rubs off on students, is more of an inward feeling than an outward appearance.
To be most effective, you'll want to save your enthusiasm for directed lessons.
But the moment you transition to giving directions or providing information, it’s best to draw down your energy.
They clap and exhort and bounce around the room trying to coax students into doing what they want, including behave, but then all but fall asleep during directed teaching.
It also demands that you know when to show enthusiasm and when to be reserved. Get these right, and your teaching will be infinitely more effective.

t: How To Handle Students Who Beg You Not To Hold Them Accountable
q: They plead. They beg. They petition. They dramatize, beseech, and implore with puppy-dog eyes.
Well, for starters, you’ll open the floodgates to more and more pleading and pressuring every time you try to enforce a consequence.
Because as soon as that student sees you thinking about it, they’re going to lay it on even thicker and heavier. And every second that passes will make it that much harder to follow through.
I wish I could, but if I let you get away with it, then I’d have to do the same for everybody else.
What still surprises me is how many students approach me later in the year to shake my hand and thank me for being fair with them.
It also makes it that much easier to say no, to follow through, to do the right thing. To be the leader they need, not the weak-kneed friend they don’t.
